visuals.title: Perpetuity growth (Gordon growth) method
visuals.formula: Terminal value = next year's cash flow ÷ (discount rate − growth rate)
visuals.note: Next year's cash flow is the first year after the forecast: the final-year cash flow × (1 + growth).

visuals.at: One hundred grown by two percent is one hundred and two
visuals.title: Cafe Group: terminal value
visuals.note: Hypothetical example. Dividing 100 instead of 102 gives about 1,430: the first trap.

visuals.at: Enterprise value about one thousand three hundred and forty
visuals.title: Cafe Group: where the value sits
visuals.note: Rounded. "Just under 400" is shown as 390. 1,460 ÷ 1.09^5 (about 1.54) ≈ 950, about 70% of the total.

visuals.at: Take growth from two percent to three
visuals.title: Same cash flow, different growth (discount rate 9%)
visuals.note: Hypothetical. 102 ÷ 7%, 103 ÷ 6%, 108 ÷ 1%. Long-term growth should stay at or below the economy's, usually 2 to 3% in developed markets.

visuals.title: Exit multiple method
visuals.formula: Terminal value = final-year EBITDA × multiple of comparable companies
visuals.note: Cafe Group: 150 × 8 = 1,200. A multiple is a growth assumption in disguise, and it carries today's market mood.

visuals.at: Our growth method gave about one thousand four hundred and sixty
visuals.title: Cross-checking the two methods
visuals.note: 1,460 is nearly 10x year-5 EBITDA of 150. Either 2% growth is generous or 8x is cautious: explain the gap, don't average it.

visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Final-year free cash flow is 200, long-term growth is 2% and the discount rate is 10%. What's the terminal value with the perpetuity growth method?
questions.explain: Grow the final year first: 200 × 1.02 = 204, then divide by 10% − 2% = 8%: 2,550. Dividing 200 instead of 204 gives 2,500, the first trap.
questions.explain_at: The formula wants next year's cash flow

questions.q: You've calculated a terminal value at the end of year five. What do you do with it before adding it to the value of the forecast years?

options.text: Grow it at the long-term rate
Add it to the forecast as it is

questions.explain: Terminal value is a value at the end of year five, so it's discounted back five years at the same rate as the forecast cash flows.
questions.explain_at: so you discount it back five years like any other cash flow

questions.q: Why shouldn't the perpetuity growth rate be above the long-run growth rate of the economy?

options.text: The company would outgrow the whole economy
The company would become too risky to value
The tax rate would rise as the company grows
Lenders would stop funding the company

questions.explain: A company growing faster than the economy forever would one day be bigger than the economy. Long-term growth usually sits at 2 to 3% in developed markets.
questions.explain_at: Nothing grows faster than the economy forever

questions.q: Terminal value is 75% of your DCF value. What do you do?

options.text: Shorten the forecast to reduce it
Switch to the exit multiple method
Accept it, test the inputs, show a range
Lower the discount rate to balance it

questions.explain: More than half is normal for a healthy company. A shorter forecast pushes even more value into the terminal value; test the growth rate, discount rate and multiple instead.
questions.explain_at: What it tells you is where to spend your time

questions.q: PTC's revenue is expected to grow about 10% a year to 2029. How do you handle that in a DCF?

options.text: Put 10% growth into the terminal value
Let growth fade before the terminal value

questions.explain: Ten percent belongs in the forecast years. Extend the forecast until growth fades towards the economy's rate, then apply the terminal value and cross-check with an exit multiple.
questions.explain_at: ten percent belongs in the forecast years
